title: Acquisition Topics DTE Assessments and DTE Sufficiency Assessments 11.3.21

cues.text: >> I'd like to welcome everyone for joining today's DAU event.
Today's episode is the DT&E assessments and DT&E sufficiency assessments.
My name is Emmett Simmons.
I'm the producer for today's event.
The agenda for today -- your microphones will be muted.
The session is being recorded, and will be posted to DAU.edu/dau-webcasts.
We are taking questions today.
Please submit your questions via the chat, and we will verbally respond
to your questions toward the end of the event.
There is a survey at the end.
We will post a survey link in the chat towards the end, and if you're here for CLPs,
please take a screenshot of the survey at the end to submit
that to your command for proof of attendance.
CLPs are pending supervisor approval,
so do you need to contact your supervisor and make sure you get approved.
So now, I'm going to turn it over to Lieutenant Colonel Chad Ryther [assumed spelling]
to introduce our speakers.
>> Good morning.
My name is Chad Ryther.
I'm a professor assistant in engineering management at DAU.
I'll be your moderator today.
Today, our speaker is Mr. William "Woody" Eischens, from the Office of Under Secretary
of Defense for Research and Engineering.
Mr. Eicschens is currently a support contractor in the developmental test and evaluation
and assessments office in the Office of the Secretary of Defense.
In this role, he supports and provides assessments
for aeronautical-related major defense acquisition programs.
Mr. Eischens has over 40 years of defense-related aeronautical test
and evaluation, product development, and project management experience,
specializing in aircraft system flight testing,
and Defense acquisition course development and delivery.
Mr. Eischens is a graduate of the U.S. air Force Test Pilot School flight Test Engineer course,
and has a Master of Science degree in aeronautics.
Before I turn it over to Mr. Eischens, we also have a special guest with us today.
Mr. Christopher Collins [assumed spelling] is the director, developmental test evaluation
and assessments within the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense.
Mr. Collins, would you like to say a few words to get us started?
>> Chad, thank you, and good morning, everyone.
Thank you for attending the day.
This is a continuation of a series of opportunities for us to talk about our efforts
within the developmental test, evaluation, and assessment organization.
We talked to you previously about our ITRA, Independent Technical Risk Assessment, efforts,
and then today, we'll focus on the test and evaluation portion.
About a year ago, the efforts for engineering and test and evaluation were merged
into one organization, and so, my organization has responsibility across both of these areas.
Look forward to your engagement.
Please, if you have any questions that this raises,
and we can't answer today, please reach out to Woody.
Also online is Mr. Orlando Flores [assumed spelling].
He is my chief engineer, and between them, we can make sure that we get you the support,
or resolve the issues that you may have related to this topic.
And so, without further ado, let me turn it over to Woody.
Thank you.
>> Thank you, sir, and welcome, everyone.
Good morning.
So developmental test and evaluation and assessments -- so what is it?
Who's the audience for it, and what would they do with it?
In T&E world, we write a lot of reports at various levels
of detail, so where does the DTA fit?
In this discussion, I hope to answer those questions, and perhaps more.
To help introduce the DTA, or developmental test and evaluation assessment,
let's first begin by reviewing the value of T&E.
Overall, the value of T&E is in creating credible,
reality-based knowledge to inform decisions.
Our focus is on informing those decisions that enable progress
in providing new or enhanced capabilities.
It isn't enough to just create knowledge information.
We also have to communicate that information for a decision-maker at the right time and in a form
that they can understand and use.
And that where is the DT&E assessment comes in.
Thank you.
The purpose of the DT&E assessment is to communicate knowledge gained from DT&E
to inform senior-level decisions.
The DTA is scoped to provide a current state of system capabilities,
and the ability of T&E to inform future decisions.
Now, what we call a DTA is actually two parts.
A DT&E assessment report, generally 10 to 15 pages, shown there on the right,
and then also an executive memorandum, around one to two pages
to summarize the report's findings and put them in the context of the decision being made.
It might be helpful really to think of this in terms of helping
to answer the three "whats" from the DTA.
What have we got, so what, in terms of the decision being made, and now what?
What should happen next?
The presentation today will start with the DTA report, and since that's really the foundation
of the developmental test and evaluation assessment, and then we'll conclude
or wrap up with a discussion of the memorandums,
and the two different types, and which ones we use when.
So, next slide, please.
The DTA is a concise assessment of system capabilities,
DT&E planning, and test resources available.
I want to emphasize the word "concise" there.
In the DT&E world, there are lots of reports written,
with most focus at the subsystem, system, or function level.
And these are written by the T&E professionals at test organizations,
and usually contain a lot of data.
It's all valuable information, but when it comes time to actually inform a decision-maker,
they don't have time to go into all that level of detail.
So the DT&E is not intended to replace all those reports.
The DTA is to summarize the results to date from the more detailed evaluations,
and put those results in the context of the decision being made,
and in a format that's useful to the decision-maker.
The DTA is written by our office, which is the Developmental Test, Evaluation,
and Assessments Office, underneath the Under Secretary of Defense for Research
and Engineering, and is written for selected key decision or knowledge points
in a major development or acquisition effort.
The DTA is written for programs following different acquisition pathways.
There is the standard, what we had in the past,
which is the major capability acquisition pathway.
The DTA also applies to middle tier acquisitions, or rapid prototyping,
or rapid fielding, software acquisition, and defense business systems,
to name just some of the six different ones that are there, that we apply to.
The DTA is a separate or independent assessment tailored
for the senior decision -- DoD decision-makers.
We want to provide a non-advocate perspective of the current state of the system under test
at a decision point, the adequacy of the T&E planning
and resources to inform future decisions.
The DTA is intended to provide an unbiased, balanced viewpoint,
and address both what the system under test can do, as well as system limitations.
The diagram there sort of shows where the DTA is trying to fit.
We're taking the data from all the testing, including modeling simulation that's been done
up to today, and trying to put an evaluation on that to then provide that information
or knowledge up to the senior decision-maker for major decision for a particular program.
Slide, please.
Now, let's get into the scope and content of a DT&E assessment.
Next slide, please.
So the DTA is organized along a typical report outline,
with the key content being there under the assessment part.
So we have a cover sheet, executive summary, system description, background,
the core area there of the assessment, and then conclusions
and recommendations, followed by references.
The core element, if you go look at the graphic there -- really, the core element of our DTA
or DT&E assessment is the capabilities.
These are the inherent capabilities of the system that we're addressing, and then, to that,
we look at how that interacts with other systems and integration,
and that includes also people integration, larger overlapping systems.
It also looks at the survivability of those capabilities in the real world,
in the mission environments, and that's both kinetic and also non-kinetic survivability.
And finally, it looks at the sustainment of those capabilities,
or ability to sustain those capabilities in the real world.
And finally, looking around the outside of that is all the T&E planning
and resource requirements necessary to do the test and evaluation.
So the question is, will we have -- is the planning in place and adequate,
and will we have the resources to be able to do the evaluation
and generate the information that's necessary for the particular decision,
or to inform the particular decision?
Now, let's step through the major sections of the DTA.
Next slide, please.
For the first really big section, the system description and background,
these are short paragraphs -- again, this overall DTA is only 10 to 15 pages or so,
so this is not intended to be a regurgitation of the entire system description.
It's supposed to summarize.
It pretty much tries to set the stage for the discussion
to follow about what the capabilities are.
So they provide a brief description of the system under test,
and how it fits into the larger mission picture.
The background paragraph is going to summarize any significant programmatic strategies
or issues that affect our ability to evaluate system capabilities or mature the system.
Here's an example of a DTA background from an actual DTA we've done in the past,
to give you a sense of the content and detail provided in the DTA.
So by design, as you can see there, it's pretty short and concise.
The intent is, again, not to repeat the more detailed description
or background available elsewhere,
but really simply set the stage for the assessment to follow.
Next slide, please.
Thank you.
The T&E planning and resources assessment section is to summarize --
look at actually both the concerns and recommendations to resolve issues.
And so, that's a key point about our assessment, is we try to make them as actionable --
so we're not just focused on finding issues of the programs and putting them out.
We also like to put recommendations out there, which actually makes those --
decision-maker could do something about it.
If they want to take action, they can take action,
but they don't necessarily mean they have to.
But they should if -- or they could if they wanted to.
So this -- the T&E planning and resources is trying to look at our ability to look
into the future and actually do the evaluations in the future,
and looking at also the resource availability.
Even though it says T&E planning, we generally try at this area to stay at the strategy level.
We're not trying to get into the detailed planning.
We're trying to look at overall strategy.
Are we looking at the right areas, and the right level of detail?
So that it's the scope and priorities that the T&E effort is undertaking,
is where we try to make our evaluation, in terms of it's going to be adequate or not.
And if not, then our recommendation could be,
what could we do to make it more adequate, or make it adequate?
So that doesn't mean, though, that we can't say that --
that we can't look at some of the more detailed planning aspects,
like the scientific test analysis technique, center of excellence, you know,
the design of experiments that is done in there.
We also want to make sure whatever we put out is -- in terms of a program, is a rigorous,
is an efficient kind of a test effort.
And those DOE-type tools do provide that efficient test plan setup,
so we want to make sure that people are -- or the programs are taking advantage of that,
in terms of coming up with a real robust and comprehensive kind of T&E effort
as part of their overall strategy.
So part of the adequacy of our T&E planning really goes into realism of the schedule, too.
So most every program that I've been associated with is very much success-oriented,
for various reasons, obviously, but we need to make sure that an assessment is --
whether that schedule optimism goes too far,
to the point that the strategy is really not executable,
meaning the T&E effort will not be able
to provide the needed information when it is needed.
And that may drive really a change to T&E strategy, if you want to try
to get the information sooner, or with fewer resources.
Maybe don't go to the level of fidelity that's required --
just various ways to try to make the T&E strategy fit, but then again,
this is the tie back to the focus on decisions and supporting decisions.
We want to make sure we get the right information to the decision-maker
at the right level of fidelity, so they can make an informed decision.
And so, that schedule realism fits into that as part of our assessment.
So common issues that we see is probably not too much of a surprise for most of us,
most of the testers listening in here.
Funding is a perennial issue.
Usually, testing is the last thing to happen in a program, so it generally suffers
from a lot of the funding constraints.
By the time you get to the testing, it doesn't happen during the planning aspects.
You might see it coming up during execution, when everything else is actually --
all the other funds have been used up, or a program's taken some cuts, and then T&E's one
of the few areas left where they can actually start taking money.
The other area is a lack of test articles.
They don't have enough test articles, or the right kind of test articles.
Test range availability is another issue.
If you want an answer -- some of the test ranges we have, obviously, are limited resources,
and so, they may not be available.
So if you want to get a test done at a certain period of time, or have a decision
at a certain point in time, you've got to make sure the ranges are available,
so you can get the testing accomplished, get the results back when they're needed.
They've got the shortfalls there -- the lack of threat-representative simulations, targets,
or expendables, things like, for example,
the electronic warfare is the classic areas that's always been sort of short.
How do you get the realistic threats in the electronic warfare area out there in the ranges?
There's always a shortfall there.
So it's continual problem, so we have to assess that, and determine is there a way around,
with modeling and simulation, or is that going to be a particular problem area that we need
to flag as making the T&E strategy not adequate.
And you see some of the other ones there.
Next slide, please.
Here's a couple of examples from T&E planning and resources.
Again, this -- you see it's pretty much of a very short kind of synopsis, summary,
of what the program has done, in terms of planning, and where we are,
in terms of our assessment of that.
In the first one, note the comment about assessing the TEMP.
It hasn't been approved yet.
The point here is that we are really focused on the actual T&E strategy, not the document.
So the fact that the document is still working its way
through the signature cycle is a minor point.
We have seen the draft, and we believe the strategy documented in the draft is adequate.
And we have the flexibility to state that as our assessment conclusion.
We're not waiting for the final signatures on a piece of paper.
It's really the -- you know, the actual strategy that you're going to try
to execute, is what we're focused on there.
Next slide, please.
System capabilities is really the area where we tend to spend most of our time
when we're doing a DT&E assessment.
This is, again, the inherent capabilities of a system.
So we're not currently trying to evaluate necessarily the program.
We're trying to evaluate the system, and what the system can do itself, the system under test.
When I mention the system, it's always the test under test,
and we're looking at typical performance capabilities.
For early assessments where the full system has not been integrated yet,
this part of the assessment could include technology maturation
or key risk reduction progress, and results in remaining issues.
For example, if you're at milestone B in a major capability acquisition,
and trying to decide whether or not to go into EMD, you don't have a full system yet.
You're just making the decision to actually integrate.
So you'd want to comment then on the technology maturation, and whether
or not the sub-technologies have matured to the point
where it's worthwhile to go into the EMD effort.
Also, although we have more confidence in results from full-scale test articles
and relevant operating environments, we do also consider results from models and simulations,
and can include that in our assessment,
if it represents the most relevant information available at this point
in the system development life cycle.
One question that often comes up is,
"Which standard of performance do we use when assessing capabilities?"
Programs have a standard of performance capture in the specifications,
and there's also a standard specified in user requirements documents,
such as capability development document, or CDD.
For example, that's the KPP or KSA threshold standard of performance.
Since our focus is on mission utility of the system,
we generally compare the actual performance to the user requirement, the KPP or KSA.
But even in this case, the fact
that a demonstrated performance did not achieve a threshold level
of performance does not automatically mean it is an issue.
For example, an EW jammer may have utility for some missions,
even if it didn't meet the KPP/KSA threshold, and we can comment on that.
Or, in some cases, some game-changing technologies, such as GPS,
may have capabilities are useful outside the originally-specified missions,
and we have the option to, again, bring that up if it's relevant to the decision being made.
One other thing to notice, that in all areas, we do also comment
on whether the stated performance requirements are evaluable, or not, or are written so vaguely
as to make any comparison with actual performance not really useful for performing --
informing the particular decision at hand.
Unfortunately, I don't have any examples to show you in this area.
All the examples we have are usually critical unclassified information,
or perhaps even classified, and I can't display that in this forum.
So next slide, please.
Integration is the next area.
Once we understand the inherent capabilities of the system under test, the next question a lot
of times that comes up is, "Well, how does this capability or this system that's under test --
how does it integrate into a larger system of systems, or some overlapping system?"
And also, how does it operate with people?
When you talk about the human factors aspects, especially from an operator perspective,
then this is an opportunity in this area to talk about that.
Interoperability is a key element in this integration issue.
It used to be a lot of the focus.
That is where the Joint Interoperability Test Command, JITC,
comes in with their certification of interoperability.
So we do touch on that, and we do address that along with things like authority
to connect, interim authorization to test.
But we wanted to really discuss more of the broader aspects of integration
with other systems and elements, including the humans factors part.
A lot of the human factors part dealing with maintenance will be handled
under the sustainment piece, but this is one area
where you might have some overlap with that.
And that's mainly to bring up a point here.
As we step through the various sections here, or various parts of the assessment,
the system capabilities, the integration, the survivability and sustainment,
those four areas generally tend to be separable.
So there's limited overlap between the four areas, which is why,
once you talk about all four of those areas, you've generally covered the waterfront,
in terms of the overall system capability and its mission utility, how it can be used
in a mission environment, or where it might have limitations that are relevant
to a particular decision that's being made at the senior level.
So that's why we have the four areas broken out the way we do.
So that's integration, and we have a couple of examples.
Next slide, please.
And you see this is the interoperability.
In the past, it was primarily the focus, and we've been expanding now on it,
but interoperability does usually take a large portion of our integration examples here.
We blacked out here the specific programs and systems to try to make this generic enough,
so that you can get, again, the gist of what we're trying to get across in this area,
how we've summarized, the level we've summarized the results at, without getting into specifics.
One thing to note, on the second example there -- I think it's about the third line down.
It says "The problem originates on the enterprise side,
and the program has submitted the papers to the appropriate agencies."
So we try to be here as -- we try to be an honest broker, and not all issues that we find,
especially when talking integration, are going to be the fault of the system under test.
So we're not going to ding the system for a problem
that somebody else -- some other system maybe has.
For example, one of my programs was airborne imagery,
and trying to get that imagery to the ships.
There was an issue onboard the ship, with the equipment onboard the ship,
where they couldn't accept the actual imagery direct.
So we had to find a workaround way, and another area was --
imagery came down to a control station on the ship,
but that control station was not integrated into the larger ship.
So they actually did a sneaker net, where they burned the imagery onto a CD,
and then ran it up to the combat information center to upload it into the ship,
to be able to use it as part of the operational picture.
So that's not necessarily a fault of the system, or the system to resolve,
but it's something that needs to be addressed.
So we comment on it here, to make sure the decision-maker's aware of how the system works,
in terms of fitting in with the larger system of systems that it's supposed to be used with.
Next slide, please.
Sustainment, and how the system or its capabilities can be sustained,
is a big area that all programs really need to look at.
It's usually the second half of, "Can it do the job?"
The second part of the question is, "Can it be sustained
and continue to do the job into the future?"
So this area summarizes their evaluation of sustainability, as specified in the TEMP,
and then our developmental evaluation framework,
usually where we capture the key components of this area.
Reliability, availability, and maintainability is a key component of this.
We also expand this out to consider things like logistics, or training, or technical orders,
the maintenance tech orders in order to maintain a particular system.
Those also are open for comment, if there's going to be particular issues in that area.
So if the system can't be sustained, a decision-maker may want to know
that before they make a decision to, say, start production, or to deploy, or not --
isn't their decision necessarily to deploy at the OSD level,
but they can influence that somewhat.
And you can see there are sustainment considerations there, and again,
we're trying to get to the "so what" in everything we've put down.
So we want to discuss the impacts of what we've seen to date,
or of any issues, in terms of mission impacts.
It's not just, oh, it's failed this many times.
It gets into the question of, "So what?"
And then, if anything, what can be done about that?
Next slide, please.
Here, we give a couple of examples.
Reliability-focused is the general way we can always talk about this, always --
everything's going to be -- have the reliability component to it, maintainability component.
So that's going to be a natural of every single VTA we actually do.
And here, we talk about if met it with exceptions.
There's a safety issue, you know, a single point of failure risk.
So you bring in risk issues, and what the impact of that is.
And again, it just sort of helps the decision-maker understand a full picture
of how the system is performing, and the risks of moving forward,
if they're applicable to the decision point at hand.
So, like, in this DTA, we may bring up general kind of cases, like this single point
of failure risk, but a particular decision in the memorandum, we may not actually bring
that particular element forward, if it doesn't have a significant impact
on the decision being made right now.
So that's one caveat I'll put there on what we put in here.
Second example, just very similar, with actual numbers.
We like to make sure when we do this, and write this in a DTA assessment,
that it's more than just opinion, that we actually back up what is written in here
with actual data that we've -- or numbers that we've captured, and we've done an evaluation
of that data to determine really what does it mean.
It can be challenging early on sometimes, especially in reliability area,
because you don't generally have a lot of hours in a lot of programs now.
We're trying to get stuff out the door quickly, so again, you can supplement this with a lot
of -- with modeling and simulations to help make an assessment then
of the significance of issues that we're finding.
And then, that can get rolled into our overall evaluation and assessment, to be --
before we actually finish up the report at a particular point in time.
Next slide, please.
Survivability is one of the final areas here.
So it's really summarizing the system's ability to survive in different threat environments.
So this includes not only the typical live fire, or kinetic survivability,
but it also includes cyber security.
It's getting a lot of attention recently.
Electronic threats, and even operating in threat environments, such as nuclear, or chem bile.
So those are all topics to be considered for a particular system
as we put together the DT&E assessment.
A lot of what the cybersecurity focus you'll see are considerations there of jumping
on cybersecurity pretty hard right now.
Again, we're trying to see, can we actually evaluate some of these requirements.
Some are written so generally and vague that it's hard to say yes or no on it,
but we try to make an assessment to the best that we can,
and compare against the user requirements the best that we can.
We like to see that the programs are using --
as part of the planning aspects, are using guidebooks.
We've put out some guidebooks.
There are other guidebooks out there,
in addition to the one we've put out on cybersecurity T&E.
There's other ones out there for live fire, and nuke, but -- so it's --
the program should not be just trying to wing it, or go it alone.
You should be using the best practices and availability of the different guidebooks
that already exist, that are out there.
And when you find issues with survivability, it's not just, oh, I got an issue.
You have to prioritize.
What is it?
How bad is it?
What does this mean, in terms of mission impact,
and ability to still complete the mission, or not?
And since our colleagues in the director operational test
and evaluation area are also very much into all the T&E that we do,
especially with survivability, since they control the live fire,
they have the responsibility of the live fire aspects of it.
We look for opportunities where we can integrate testing with them.
Again, cybersecurity and with the live fire, a lot of times, you don't --
a lot of systems don't do the full-scale live fire testing.
So we end up doing coupon-level testing, and that's a lot -- very strong into DT&E world.
And so, we comment then on what the results of the live fire coupon tests are.
Next slide, please.
Here's a couple examples from the live fire survivability perspective.
And cybersecurity, obviously, is one that we talked about there.
So it talks about who's doing what, and what they're finding with it.
Live fire is an example of a live fire kind of comment,
and again, talked about the coupon test.
So one of the big issues generally with live fire is the hydrodynamic ram.
So you shoot at a fuel tank with a kinetic round,
and then you see what the pressure wave does.
Does it blow out the tank and leak fuel, flammable liquids all over the place
that could get sparked and ignite?
And you can see the other example right there, so, couple quick examples, anyway.
Next slide, please.
Exit criteria is another aspect when you talk about major decisions in programs,
like major capability acquisition.
You have your milestone B, and especially at milestone C, your initial production decision.
Usually milestone B ADM, acquisition decision memorandum, will include various exit criteria
for getting into the production decision.
So when we discuss those, we don't have a separate section that talks about exit criteria,
because usually they show up in either the system capability area, or integration,
or survivability, or sustainment.
Usually, they're in one of those four areas anyway.
So we say let's talk about them in those particular points.
And if we do have the opportunity for a particular decision point
to recommend exit criteria for a future decision, we can do that, and again,
that would be part of one of those other four areas.
But we do want to make sure that the exit criteria we actually recommend
is program-specific.
It's clear, and it's measurable.
So there's no, you know, "do good stuff."
It's really, "no, show this level of performance."
And we like to also get to the results-focused part of an exit criteria, not just activity,
don't fly much hours, or conduct a bunch of missions, just a number of missions.
Demonstrate actual kind of performance if we're going to recommend a particular exit criteria.
So, next slide, please.
So that's the actual DTA report.
That's really the foundation of our assessment.
However, the defense acquisition executive
or service acquisition executives are usually our customers here of the DTA.
They don't have time to read even 10 to 15 pages, so they're looking
for a very shortened version that they can quickly get the gist of what do we find
that has an impact on the decision they're making.
So what we try to do is bring forward the key findings, or describing the risk to the decision
at hand, and we do that in the form of short memorandums.
And then, in addition to that, we attach the full report, so that it's really more
for the PEO, the program manager, others to really understand the risks
that we've identified, and it fleshes it out a little bit more in more detail.
So they can then take action on it, or they can come back and discuss it with us
if they have questions, go forward.
There's two types of transmittal memorandums.
There is the developmental test and evaluation assessment, and the developmental test
and evaluation sufficiency assessment memorandum.
So let's get into discussing both of those, and when they're used,
and the typical content in those.
The first one we hit -- I'll call it -- it's the DTSA, the DT&E sufficiency assessment,
is a statutory requirement, came out in the NDAA for 2018 --
for fiscal year 2018, and it requires the DTSA for MDAPS, major defense acquisition programs,
at two milestones, milestone B and milestone C. And this probably cues you into the fact that,
well, we didn't have the different acquisition pathways, but by just saying milestone B
and milestone C, we're really talking primarily the major capability acquisition pathway,
in this case.
It did modify the Title 10 and the certifications required at milestone B
and milestone C that requires a brief summary report to Congress, which --
the statement says we need, say, summary of DT&E sufficiency assessment.
So that generally becomes a one- or two-liner, or maybe a short paragraph,
whereas the actual memo we have could be a page or two.
So you've gone from a 10 to 15-page report to a one- to two-page memo,
to what Congress sees is a few lines.
So the focus, again, is be concise, get to the point, and not a lot of time for a lot
of extraneous discussion around this.
The statutory did state what the minimum content was for sufficiency assessments,
and there is guidance that was put out by OSD, in terms of how to write those.
And the content -- specifically what kind of content would go in the two-pager.
The DTSA is written by -- and this is a language that's in the law --
"the senior official responsible for DT&E in the Office of Secretary of Defense for ACAT 1D,
and that, no surprise, is the DTE&A office.
Mr. Collins, being the director, is the one responsible for putting that together.
And then, for where -- if it's ACAT 1B or 1C,
where the service provides a milestone decision authority, or MDA, the SAE is that then it's
over to the service official responsible for DT&E.
So usually, let's say in an Air Force program, the Air Force TE,
or the same for those other services that are out there.
Next slide, please.
Didn't pop over.
Oh, I'm sorry, it did.
